points: Crude birth rate: live births per 1,000 people per year.
Crude death rate: deaths per 1,000 people per year.
Natural change: birth rate minus death rate. A positive result is natural increase; a negative result is natural decrease.
Net migration: immigrants minus emigrants.
Total fertility rate: the average number of children per woman.
Replacement level: a total fertility rate of about 2.1 children per woman in developed countries, the level at which a population replaces itself.
Infant mortality rate: deaths of children under one year old per 1,000 live births.
Life expectancy: the average number of years a newborn is expected to live.
Population change equals natural change plus net migration. In any period between two censuses, the larger of the two components explains the growth or decline.
The census is a count of every person on one night. In Ireland it is held every five years and run by the Central Statistics Office (CSO).
The Irish census records age, sex, place of residence, birthplace, nationality, religion, ethnicity, Irish language, housing, work and commuting.

Census 2016 to Census 2022: the population grew by about 360,000 (about 7.6%). Natural increase contributed about 170,000 and net migration about 190,000, so net migration was the slightly larger component.
The 1926 census was the first held by the Irish Free State.
The 1976 census was cancelled; a special census was held in 1979 instead.
The 2001 census was postponed to 2002 by foot-and-mouth disease.
The 2021 census was postponed to 2022 by COVID-19 and held on 3 April 2022.
Planning schools, hospitals and housing: counts of children, patients and households show where services are needed.
Pensions: the age structure sets the cost of pensions; the State pension age has been 66 since 2014.
Transport and infrastructure: population size and location show where roads, rail and water services are needed.
Constituency boundaries: the population of each constituency determines the number of TDs it elects.
Funding and workforce planning: funding is allocated to regions by population, and population forecasts show future labour supply and the need for workers from abroad.

notes.b: Distribution is where people live. Density is the number of people per square kilometre of land.
points: Density = population ÷ area in km².
Illustrative example (invented figures): a region of 400 km² with 120,000 people has a density of 120,000 ÷ 400 = 300 people per km².
Relief: lowlands attract more people than high mountains, which are costly to farm and build on.
Climate: temperate climates support dense settlement; places that are too hot, too cold or too dry have fewer people.
Soils and water supply: fertile soils and reliable water support farming and settlement.
Natural resources: coalfields drew industrial populations in the 19th century.
Economic opportunity: jobs attract people, and regions with few jobs lose their young people.
Transport routes: roads, rail lines and navigable water attract settlement along them.
Cities and ports: cities and ports offer jobs and services, so they draw large populations.
History: colonial ports and plantations shaped where people settled.
Government policy: policy can direct population into or out of particular areas.
High, steep or cold land is difficult to farm, build on and reach.
Deserts and dense forest offer little water, farmland or access.
Poor soils and remoteness limit farming, and remote areas lack markets and services.
Few jobs cause young people to leave, so the population falls and density drops.
Dense: East Asia, South Asia, Europe, the north-eastern USA and the Nile valley.
Sparse: the Sahara, the Amazon Basin, Siberia, northern Canada, Greenland and Antarctica.
About 90% of the world's people live in the northern hemisphere.
Most people live near coasts and rivers.
Dense core: the Benelux countries, the Rhine–Ruhr, south-east England, the Po valley and the Paris region.
Sparse periphery: northern Scandinavia, the Scottish Highlands and interior Spain.
The Netherlands has over 500 people per km² (2020s), one of Europe's most densely populated countries.
The EU average is about 110 people per km² (2020s).

Slow growth, stagnation or decline: Europe and East Asia.

notes.b: The model shows how birth and death rates, and so population growth, change as a country develops.
points: Birth rate high, death rate high, and little growth.
Example: no country is in stage 1 today; the best examples are pre-industrial societies.
Birth rate high; death rate falling rapidly, and the death rate falls most in this stage; growth is rapid.
The death rate falls because of clean water and sanitation, vaccination, a better food supply and medical care.
Example: Niger, described below.
Birth rate falling; death rate low; growth slows.
Example: India, with a total fertility rate of about 2.0 (2019–21).
Birth rate low, death rate low, and little growth.
Examples: Ireland and the USA. Ireland is in stage 4.
Birth rate below death rate, so natural change is negative (natural decrease) and the population falls.
Examples: Germany, Italy and Japan.
Niger is a West African, landlocked country, largely in the Sahel and Sahara.
Population is about 27 million (2023), growing by over 3% a year (early 2020s).
Total fertility rate is about 6 children per woman (early 2020s), among the highest in the world.
Median age is about 15, among the lowest in the world.
Its population pyramid has a very wide base.

Japan has the world's oldest population: about 29% of people are aged 65 or over (2023), the highest share in the world.
Population peaked at about 128 million around 2008–2010, was about 124 million in 2024, and is falling.
Total fertility rate is about 1.2 (2023).
Few immigrants by European standards.

notes.h: Why the birth rate falls after stage 2
points: Female education and paid work: women have later and fewer children.
Contraception is widely available.
Falling infant mortality removes the need for 'insurance' births, as parents can expect their children to survive.
Urbanisation: children cost more and earn less in towns and cities.
Pensions replace children as old-age security.
Later marriage, and weaker religious influence on family size.
Challenges: a shrinking workforce, labour shortages, rising pension and health costs, closing schools and rural depopulation.
Responses: immigration, pro-natalist incentives to raise birth rates, and later retirement.
The model is based on European experience.
It ignores migration.
Developing countries' death rates fell much faster than Europe's, because medicine was imported, so their growth has been faster.
Some countries may not complete the transition, and it has no fixed time scale.
A population pyramid shows age cohorts in five-year bands, with males on the left and females on the right, as percentages or numbers.
Uses: planning services, forecasting future needs, comparing countries, and showing past events such as baby booms, wars and emigration.
Wide base and narrow top: high fertility and short life expectancy, as in Niger.
Straight sides: a stable population with low birth and death rates.
Narrow base and wide top (top-heavy): an ageing population, as in Japan.
A developed country's pyramid is typically straight-sided or top-heavy, while a developing country's is wide-based.
Bulges show baby booms or immigration of young adults.
Notches show emigration, low birth years or war.
More women than men at the oldest ages, because women live longer.
Dependency ratio = (people aged 0–14 + people aged 65 and over) ÷ people aged 15–64 × 100.
Young dependency ratio = people aged 0–14 ÷ people aged 15–64 × 100. Old-age dependency ratio = people aged 65 and over ÷ people aged 15–64 × 100.
Illustrative example (invented figures): 30,000 aged 0–14, 10,000 aged 65 and over and 80,000 aged 15–64 give (30,000 + 10,000) ÷ 80,000 × 100 = 50.
Urban dependency ratios are usually lower than rural ones.
Young working adults migrate to cities for jobs and college, leaving older people, and sometimes children, in rural areas.
Higher pension costs.
More demand for health care, nursing homes and carers.
A smaller tax base from fewer workers.
Pressure to raise the pension age.
Changing housing and transport needs.
Planning responses in Ireland: home-care supports, pension reform, more geriatric services, encouraging immigration of workers, and age-friendly towns.

notes.h: Effects of a high young dependency ratio
points: Demand for schools, maternity and child health care, and for future jobs and housing.
A future workforce, the basis of the demographic dividend discussed in Overpopulation.
Income and economic development: birth rates fall as income rises.
Status and education of women: educated women with status tend to have fewer children.
Religion and culture.
Access to contraception.
Government policy.
Infant mortality: high infant mortality encourages larger families.
Urban or rural living: rural families tend to have more children.
Medical technology: vaccines and antibiotics.
Sanitation, diet, income and health services.
Lifestyle diseases such as heart disease and cancer are the main causes of death in rich countries.
Conflict, famine and disease, such as malaria and HIV/AIDS, are the main causes of death in poor countries.

notes.h: How fertility and mortality change structure
points: Falling fertility narrows the base of the pyramid.
Rising life expectancy widens the top of the pyramid.
The result is an older population with a higher median age.

notes.h: Raising life expectancy in a country such as Niger
points: Clean water and sanitation.
Vaccination.
Mosquito nets and malaria treatment.
More doctors and clinics.
Better nutrition.
Female education.

notes.h: Why life expectancy is long in Ireland
points: A good diet and housing.
Effective health services and vaccination.
Clean water.

Safer work.

notes.h: Births and fertility in Ireland since the 1950s
points: Fertility was high into the 1970s, with Catholic culture, large families and little access to contraception.
Births peaked at about 74,000 in 1980.
The total fertility rate was about 4 in the early 1970s, fell below replacement level around 1990, and was about 1.5 in 2023.
Births were about 55,000 in 2023 against about 35,000 deaths, giving natural increase of about 20,000.
Free secondary education, introduced in 1967 by Donogh O'Malley, and more women in third-level education.
The marriage bar, which forced women in the public service to resign on marriage, was removed in 1973.
Contraception was legalised by the Health (Family Planning) Act 1979, on prescription; access was widened in 1985 and the early 1990s.
More women in paid employment, later marriage and later first births.
Secularisation, and the cost of housing and childcare.

Heavy net emigration in the 1950s and 1980s; net emigration of about 400,000 between 1951 and 1961, which the 1954 Report of the Commission on Emigration and Other Population Problems examined.
Net immigration in the 1970s, from the mid-1990s to 2008, and again from the mid-2010s.

factCards.term: Census 2016 to 2022: natural increase or net migration?
factCards.definition: Population change = natural change + net migration. Between 2016 and 2022 the population grew by about 360,000 (about 7.6%): natural increase about 170,000 and net migration about 190,000, so net migration was slightly larger.

factCards.term: How governments use population statistics: name six uses
factCards.definition: Planning schools, hospitals and housing; pensions (the State pension age has been 66 since 2014); transport and infrastructure; constituency boundaries, as population sets the number of TDs; funding for regions and workforce planning.

factCards.term: Low population density: four reasons
factCards.definition: High, steep or cold land is hard to farm, build on and reach; deserts and dense forest offer little water, farmland or access; poor soils and remoteness; few jobs, so young people leave and density drops.

factCards.term: Ireland's population distribution: Census 2022 figures
factCards.definition: State about 5.15 million, about 73 people per km²; Greater Dublin Area (Dublin, Meath, Kildare, Wicklow) about 2.1 million, about 40% of the total; Co. Dublin about 1,600 per km²; Mayo about 25 per km²; Leitrim and Roscommon also sparse.

factCards.term: Ireland's distribution over time, and why density is rising
factCards.definition: Before the Famine the population was rural and weighted to the west; now it is eastern and urban, with fast growth in Meath, Kildare and Wicklow. Density rises because natural increase and net immigration since the 1990s add people to a fixed area.

factCards.term: World population growth: the pattern and the contrast
factCards.definition: Slow until about 1800 (about 1 billion), then a J-curve driven by falling death rates, reaching 8 billion on 15 November 2022; now slowing. Global fertility about 2.3 (early 2020s), down from about 5 in the 1950s. Growth is fastest in sub-Saharan Africa.

factCards.term: Demographic Transition Model: the five stages with examples
factCards.definition: Stage 1 high stationary: pre-industrial societies (no country today). Stage 2 early expanding, when the death rate falls most: Niger. Stage 3 late expanding: India. Stage 4 low stationary: Ireland, USA. Stage 5 declining: Germany, Italy, Japan.

factCards.term: DTM stage 2: why the death rate falls
factCards.definition: Clean water and sanitation; vaccination; a better food supply; medical care. The death rate falls fastest in stage 2 while the birth rate stays high, so growth is rapid.

factCards.term: DTM: why the birth rate falls after stage 2
factCards.definition: Female education and paid work; contraception; falling infant mortality, so fewer insurance births; urbanisation, as children cost more and earn less; pensions replace children as old-age security; later marriage; weaker religious influence.

factCards.term: DTM stage 5 countries: challenges and responses
factCards.definition: Challenges: a shrinking workforce, labour shortages, rising pension and health costs, closing schools, rural depopulation. Responses: immigration, pro-natalist incentives to raise birth rates, later retirement.

factCards.term: Population pyramids: uses and how to read them
factCards.definition: Uses: planning services, forecasting needs, comparing countries, showing past events. Reading: bulges show baby booms or immigration of young adults; notches show emigration, low birth years or war; more women than men at the oldest ages.

factCards.term: Pyramid shapes: developing vs developed countries
factCards.definition: Wide base, narrow top: high fertility and short life expectancy (Niger). Straight sides: stable, low birth and death rates. Narrow base, wide top: ageing (Japan). Falling fertility narrows the base and longer lives widen the top.

factCards.term: Why urban dependency ratios are lower than rural ones
factCards.definition: Young working adults migrate to cities for jobs and college, leaving older people, and sometimes children, behind in rural areas, so rural areas have more dependants for every person of working age.

factCards.term: Ageing population: effects and planning responses in Ireland
factCards.definition: Effects: higher pension costs; more demand for health care, nursing homes and carers; a smaller tax base; pressure to raise the pension age. Responses: home-care supports, pension reform, geriatric services, immigrant workers, age-friendly towns.

factCards.term: Birth rates: factors that influence them
factCards.definition: Income and economic development; the status and education of women; religion and culture; access to contraception; government policy; infant mortality, as high rates encourage larger families; urban or rural living.

factCards.term: Death rates: factors in rich and poor countries
factCards.definition: Medical technology (vaccines, antibiotics), sanitation, diet, income and health services. Rich countries: lifestyle diseases such as heart disease and cancer. Poor countries: conflict, famine and disease such as malaria and HIV/AIDS.

factCards.term: Life expectancy: why it is long in Ireland and how to raise it in Niger
factCards.definition: Ireland (about 82–83 years): good diet and housing, health services, vaccination, clean water, fewer smokers, safer work. Niger: clean water and sanitation, vaccination, mosquito nets and malaria treatment, more clinics, better nutrition, female education.

factCards.term: Ireland's census population, 1841 to 2022: key figures
factCards.definition: 1841: about 6.5 million; 1851: 5.1 million; 1926: 3.0 million; 1961: 2.8 million, the lowest ever; 1981: 3.4 million; a small fall 1986 to 1991; 2002: 3.9 million; 2016: 4.76 million; 2022: about 5.15 million, the first time over 5 million since 1851.

factCards.term: Irish births and fertility since the 1970s: key figures
factCards.definition: Fertility about 4 in the early 1970s; births peaked at about 74,000 in 1980; fertility fell below replacement around 1990 and was about 1.5 in 2023, with about 55,000 births and 35,000 deaths (natural increase about 20,000).

factCards.term: Why Irish fertility fell: six reasons (three with dates)
factCards.definition: Free secondary education (1967, Donogh O'Malley) and more women at third level; marriage bar removed (1973); contraception legalised (Health (Family Planning) Act 1979); more women in paid work and later marriage; secularisation; housing and childcare costs.

factCards.term: Ireland since the 1950s: migration and urbanisation in brief
factCards.definition: Heavy net emigration in the 1950s (about 400,000 between 1951 and 1961) and again in the 1980s; net immigration in the 1970s, from the mid-1990s to 2008 and from the mid-2010s. Census 1971 was the first with a town majority; about 63% urban by 2016. Households are smaller.

factCards.term: Ireland's changing age structure: Census 2022
factCards.definition: About 776,000 aged 65 and over (about 15%), up about 22% since 2016; average age 38.8, up from 37.4 in 2016; about one-fifth under 15; about one in five people (just over 1 million) born outside Ireland.

factCards.term: Europe's ageing population: the EU, Germany, Italy and Bulgaria
factCards.definition: EU (2023): fertility about 1.4, median age about 44.5, about 21% aged 65+, so immigration supplies most growth. Germany: deaths above births every year since 1972. Italy: fertility about 1.2. Bulgaria: about 9 million (1989) to 6.5 million (2021).

factCards.term: Niger: a young, fast-growing population (DTM stage 2)
factCards.definition: Landlocked West Africa, in the Sahel and Sahara; about 27 million (2023), growing over 3% a year; fertility about 6 and median age about 15, among the most extreme in the world; a very wide-based pyramid; most people live in the rainier south.

factCards.term: Japan: an old, shrinking population (DTM stage 5)
factCards.definition: About 29% aged 65 or over (2023), the world's highest share; population peaked at about 128 million around 2008–2010 and was about 124 million in 2024; fertility about 1.2; few immigrants; a top-heavy pyramid.

questions.prompt: Describe and explain how the characteristics of Ireland's population have changed since the 1950s.
questions.model: Size: the State's population fell at almost every census from 1841 (about 6.5 million) to a low of about 2.8 million in 1961, then grew to about 5.15 million in 2022, above 5 million for the first time since 1851. Births and fertility: fertility was high into the 1970s, with Catholic culture, large families and little access to contraception, and births peaked at about 74,000 in 1980. Fertility fell below replacement around 1990 and was about 1.5 in 2023, because of free secondary education (1967), the removal of the marriage bar (1973), legal contraception (1979), women's paid work, later marriage and the cost of housing and childcare. Deaths and life expectancy: life expectancy rose to about 82–83 years, women live about 4 years longer than men, and infant mortality fell to about 3 per 1,000 live births. Migration: heavy net emigration in the 1950s and 1980s, net immigration in the 1970s, from the mid-1990s to 2008 and from the mid-2010s; net migration was the larger component of growth between 2016 and 2022. Age structure: the population has moved from a young, wide-based pyramid to an ageing one; about 776,000 people (about 15%) were aged 65 and over in 2022, and the average age rose from 37.4 in 2016 to 38.8 in 2022. Distribution: the population has moved east and to towns; towns held more people than rural areas from 1971, about 63% of people were urban in 2016, and the Greater Dublin Area holds about 40% of the population.

questions.prompt: Examine how changing fertility and mortality rates impact on population structure, with reference to example(s) you have studied.
questions.model: Falling fertility narrows the base of the population pyramid, rising life expectancy widens the top, and the result is an older population with a higher median age. The Demographic Transition Model links these changes: in stage 2 high birth rates and falling death rates widen the base as the young population grows, and in stage 5 birth and death rates are low and the population falls. Niger (stage 2): the pyramid has a very wide base, the total fertility rate is about 6 children per woman, the median age is about 15 and growth is over 3% a year, so most people are young. Japan (stage 5): the pyramid is top-heavy, with a narrow base and a wide top; about 29% of people are aged 65 or over (2023), the population has fallen from a peak of about 128 million to about 124 million (2024), and the total fertility rate is about 1.2. Ireland: the pyramid has moved from a young, wide-based shape, when fertility was high into the 1970s, to an ageing one, because fertility fell below replacement around 1990 and life expectancy rose. In 2022 about one-fifth of the population was under 15 and about 15% was aged 65 or over, showing the shift from youth to age.

questions.prompt: Explain briefly the term natural change.
questions.model: Natural change is the birth rate minus the death rate: natural increase when births exceed deaths, and natural decrease when deaths exceed births.

questions.prompt: State one reason why the birth rate falls after stage 2 of the DTM.
questions.model: Women gain education and paid work, so they have later and fewer children.

questions.prompt: Explain briefly one challenge facing countries in stage 5 of the DTM.
questions.model: A shrinking workforce creates labour shortages, while pension and health costs rise as the population ages.
